en.content:
Tai Po’s Wang Fuk Court fire remains a reminder that disaster prevention is as much about governance details as it is about emergency response. The administrator’s stated confidence in convening an owners’ meeting next month—after missing an earlier deadline—reflects the practical reality of stalled consensus in post-incident management. Yet for residents who lost homes, trust cannot be rebuilt through assurances alone. Clear timelines, transparent documentation of safety decisions, and consistent communication with owners are indispensable, because rebuilding is not simply a construction task; it is also a process of accountability that must be felt at ground level.

A broader lesson, highlighted by fire-safety commentary, is the need to treat external building works as a risk chain rather than an afterthought. Decisions about combustibles, façade materials, and site practices may appear technical, but they determine how quickly a fire can spread beyond the origin point. That perspective is especially important in Hong Kong’s dense housing context, where vertical and external exposure make containment harder and evacuation more urgent. The government and responsible parties should therefore keep prevention measures specific—what materials are banned, what standards apply, what inspections will occur, and how non-compliance will be enforced—rather than relying on general reminders after tragedies.

At the same time, residents’ concerns about procedure and fairness deserve a calm but firm response. When disaster recovery drags, people naturally question whether they are being served, whether costs are being managed responsibly, and whether decision-making reflects their lived experience. The owners’ meeting, therefore, should not be viewed as a box-ticking exercise, but as a forum where technical findings, remediation plans, and funding arrangements are openly explained. Such engagement can reduce conflict and make safety upgrades more durable—because when people understand the “why” behind safety work, they are more likely to support the “how.”

In today’s environment—where public attention is also split across external crises and regional security concerns—local tragedies like Wang Fuk Court can easily become background noise. But the value of a good society lies in how it handles pain close to home. Ensuring prompt, accountable post-fire governance and setting rigorous external safety standards will not only lower future risk; it will also demonstrate that Hong Kong’s systems can learn and act with discipline, not just react with urgency.
en.topic_title: Tai Po fire: Wang Fuk Court administrator ‘confident’ owners meeting can be held next month

zh.content:
今日本港最值得關注的，不是天災、意外或外地戰略新聞，而係本地嘅生活成本急升：港燈宣布由7月起上調燃料附加費，幅度高達33.9%，理由係「中東戰事」帶來嘅「遞延影響」。呢個數字一落地，唔少家庭都會即刻計到「每月會多咗幾多」；對長者、基層同用電量較高嘅住戶嚟講，分分鐘就係實實在在嘅壓力。電費唔係奢侈品，係日常必需品——所以每一次附加費上調，政府同營運商都必須以更高透明度交代，否則就會令社會只剩下「被動承擔」嘅感覺。

不過，亦要承認，燃料成本確實會受國際局勢影響，香港作為高度依賴能源進口嘅地方，未必可以完全「脫鉤」。真正嘅爭點，唔喺於要唔要反映外部成本，而係反映成本嘅同時，責任分配同監管要唔要到位：點解係以呢個機制、呢個時間點、呢個幅度去上調？有冇將任何可控嘅因素（例如營運效率、採購策略、減少不必要開支）先行吸收，先至轉嫁？仲有，所謂「遞延效應」到底遞延咗啲咩、計算基準係咩、公共可查程度幾多？如果市民連計法都追唔到，就容易令公眾覺得附加費變成「自動調整」，而唔係「有理有據嘅平衡」。

在立場上，我認為當局同電力公司可以同時做到兩樣嘢：一方面承認外部市場波動嘅現實，另一方面就必須用更明確嘅成本解釋、定期核對同必要嘅紓緩措施，減低對市民嘅打擊。尤其今次幅度偏大，更需要配套，例如針對低收入家庭嘅電費支援、加快檢視費率/附加費機制嘅合理性，或者至少要提供更可視化、可審計嘅數據（例如成本構成、對沖安排、匯率同燃料價格變動對應關係）。否則「上調係因為國際局勢」就會變成一種免責口徑，長遠會削弱社會對公共服務定價嘅信任。

最後，呢件事其實提醒咗香港：能源轉型同能源韌性，唔係口號，而係會直接落到每一個家庭嘅電費單。若只係一次又一次把波動成本「遞延、再遞延」轉嫁，市民感受只會愈來愈強烈。真正有深度嘅做法係，把短期成本管理同長期結構改革捆綁起來——用制度去提高透明度、用政策去對沖弱勢影響、用規劃去減少未來對單一燃料價格週期嘅敏感度。咁樣，社會先至會明白：承擔唔等於被動接受，而係公平分擔同負責任嘅調節。
zh.topic_title: HK Electric to hike fuel surcharge by 33.9% from July over ‘deferred effect’ of war in Middle East
